title: ULPower Valve Cover
subtitle: Reverse-engineered aircraft engine valve cover, built at Dassault Systèmes
summary: Reverse-engineered a missing ULPower aircraft engine valve cover from calipers and reference photos into a production-ready CAD model.
why_md: While I was working on-site at Dassault Systèmes, I got handed a missing ULPower aircraft engine valve cover and asked to bring it back. This wasn't a 'go buy a replacement' job; buying one simply wasn't an option. It had to be rebuilt from scratch using nothing but measurements, reference photos, and whatever I could translate into an accurate, manufacturable CAD model. And it wasn't enough to just copy the shape. The file had to be clean enough to drop straight into the prototyping and production pipeline without anyone touching it up.
how_md: Capturing the geometry took a mix of precision and guesswork. I took every dimension I could reach with a set of calipers, then leaned on photos to model the subtle curves, the embossed lettering, and the gasket sealing surfaces. Because this was going on an aircraft engine, I had to keep real-world stuff in mind the whole time: vibration, thermal expansion, and how much material would come off during machining. Before I handed anything off, I printed a prototype in PLA+ on my Ender 3 V2 Neo to check that the fit and alignment were actually right.
problems_md: The finished model matched the original in form, function, and tolerance, and it was ready to manufacture as-is. This one really drove home that I can bridge physical measurements and digital modeling while thinking a few steps ahead to how the part has to survive out in the real world. It also showed I can work inside tight constraints and still deliver something that holds up to both engineering and production standards.

title: Monitor Mount
subtitle: FEA-driven mount for a 7.1 kg, 31.5″ display
summary: An FEA-driven monitor mount: 8 iterations to a factor of safety of 2–5 and under 0.3 mm displacement carrying a 7.1 kg display.
why_md: I built this mount to hold a 7.1 kg, 31.5-inch Acer monitor while keeping the ports easy to get at. It started as a simple block that locked the monitor at 90 degrees, but I wanted to be able to swivel it up when I needed to. I knew from the start that PETG would be plenty strong, so the real challenge became the balance: how do I cut as much weight as I can and still keep a high factor of safety?
how_md: My first simulation showed a solid PETG block would shrug off the weight, so I started pulling material out in controlled ways. Triangular supports set about three millimeters off the walls carried the load well, and the extra cutouts I added actually improved how the force spread out. To really lean on it, I ran a study with 100 newtons pushing from the top and another 100 newtons pulling through the hinge pin. Most of the results came back blue and light green, so I had plenty of margin, with just one small stress spot on a single triangle. Instead of dumping more infill in, I simplified the geometry and cut a triangle out behind the hinge hole, which made it stronger without adding a gram. I was also worried a single screw wouldn't hold up to the twisting force, so I added a second one and spread them apart to share the load. After a few more rounds I rethought where the hinge sat and found a spot that gave me a much cleaner load path.
problems_md: After eight iterations and a lot of simulations, the mount held a factor of safety between two and five every time. Max displacement came out to 0.3 millimeters on the wall piece and 0.02 millimeters on the screen mount, well inside the safe zone. The whole thing reinforced how I like to work: **simplify, then lighten**. Pull out anything that isn't doing work, reinforce only where the data says it's weak, and trust what the numbers tell you. The final mount is light, reliable, and holds my monitor exactly where I want it.

title: Raspberry Pi Laptop
subtitle: A SolidWorks-designed Linux laptop on a Raspberry Pi
summary: A fully functional Linux laptop built on a Raspberry Pi, with five hinge iterations before the screen sat exactly right.
why_md: This one started as a SolidWorks class project, but I treated it like a real product from day one. The goal was a fully working Linux laptop running on a Raspberry Pi, something practical, affordable, and portable that didn't feel like a rough prototype held together with hope. I wanted a clean enclosure that hid its cables inside, kept them from tangling, and still gave me access to every port I needed. It was never about cramming parts into a box; I wanted a whole system that worked reliably and actually looked the part.
how_md: The hinge turned out to be the hardest problem in the whole build. It took five separate iterations before I got one that could hold the screen at different angles without wobbling and still fold shut smoothly. On the inside I had to lay out the Pi, the battery, and the display so nothing pulled on a cable and every port lined up with its opening in the enclosure. I did most of the CAD and R&D myself, from the main body and lid geometry (shaped to move air through it) down to the mounting features and the internal cable channels.
problems_md: The finished laptop was compact, booted straight up, and felt solid in my hands. It proved to me that I can take a project from an idea all the way to a working object while juggling usability, manufacturability, and how it looks. More than that, it showed I can pull CAD, mechanical problem-solving, and hands-on assembly into one build that works as well on the desk as it does on paper.

title: Carbon Filter Fume Extractor
subtitle: A $5 carbon-filter fume extractor that beat the commercial unit
summary: A compact carbon-filter fume extractor built for about $5 that outperformed commercial units at roughly 10× the price.
why_md: I built this compact carbon-filter fume extractor to fix a real problem in my home workshop: bad ventilation every time I sat down to solder. The cheap commercial options were underpowered and still cost too much, so I figured I'd just design and build one out of stuff I already had lying around. I wanted it small, efficient, and reliable, with a few design choices that made it easy to keep clean.
how_md: The first version had a stand so I could angle it, but testing showed the fan pulled fumes fine from four inches away without me repositioning anything, so the stand had to go. Dropping it simplified the build and made it print better too. I started with a 12 V fan and a voltage booster, but it kept failing on me during testing (the multimeter confirmed I was overstressing the parts), so I swapped in a 5 V USB-C fan. That cut the electrical load, cleaned up the wiring, and let me throw out the problematic booster circuit entirely.
problems_md: The finished extractor beat the commercial units I compared it against, cost me about five dollars to build, and is easy to service if it ever needs it. The bigger takeaway for me was seeing how much a small design change can move performance, and getting comfortable blending airflow, electronics troubleshooting, and structure into one thing that actually balances.

title: OctoPi Laptop Enclosure
subtitle: A dedicated OctoPi control station for 3D-printer management
summary: A portable, single-purpose OctoPi enclosure that packs the Pi, a display, a camera, and cooling into one compact unit.
why_md: I wanted a portable, dedicated station for running OctoPi so I could manage my 3D printer without tying up my main computer. My Raspberry Pi laptop gave me the starting point, so I reworked that idea into a single-purpose device built just for print control. It needed to be compact, tough, and organized, with everything living in one unit I could move around the workspace without a hassle.
how_md: I designed the enclosure to hold the Pi, a display, a camera module, and cooling vents while keeping the footprint as small as I could get it. Cable routing went straight into the design so nothing tangled and setup or servicing stayed easy. I reinforced the hinge mounts so the lid could open and close over and over without wearing out. Every mounting point, vent, and cable channel got placed with reliability and ease of use in mind.
problems_md: The finished enclosure turned into a mobile printer hub that cleaned up my whole workflow and kept my setup organized. It showed I can take an existing design and adapt it into a specialized tool that does its one job better, without letting build quality or usability slip.

title: Filament Recycler
subtitle: Closing the loop on 3D-printing waste
summary: A beginner-friendly filament recycler that turns printing waste back into usable filament, from basic PLA to abrasive carbon blends.
why_md: 3D printing is great until you look at the pile of wasted plastic it leaves behind: failed prints, support material, leftover spools that can't be reused without the right gear. I want to flip that problem on its head. This concept is a beginner-friendly, low-maintenance filament recycler that works with any material, from basic PLA all the way to the abrasive carbon blends.
how_md: The plan is a rugged metal hopper that can take heavy use, feeding into a hardened shredder and then through a precisely heated extrusion system. The trick is keeping it simple enough for a maker to run without a manual, but robust enough to chew through different plastics without constant maintenance or pricey replacement parts.
problems_md: If it works, 3D-printing waste stops being trash and turns into a resource loop instead. That makes the whole process cheaper and a lot easier on the planet, whether you're a hobbyist printing on the weekend or running a shop full of machines.

title: Automatic Hydroponic System
subtitle: Arduino-based precision agriculture for small-scale growers
summary: An Arduino automation unit handling EC sensing, pH tracking, and nutrient dosing for hydroponics.
why_md: Hydroponics lives and dies on precision. If your nutrient levels are off, your plants either stall out or burn. Checking EC and dosing nutrients by hand gets old fast, especially once you've got a few systems running at once. My concept is an Arduino-based unit that handles all of it: EC sensing, pH tracking, and nutrient dosing through a set of small pumps.
how_md: The probes would be modular so they're easy to swap out, and all the electronics would sit in a sealed enclosure to survive the humidity. I want it to learn your system's rhythm over time and adjust its dosing based on where the plants are in their growth and what the environment is doing. The goal is real set-it-and-forget-it automation, the kind that actually pushes your yields up instead of just keeping things alive.
problems_md: The whole point is to put precision growing within reach of small growers, cut the crop loss that comes from nutrient swings, and hand people back the time they'd otherwise spend babysitting probes.

title: AI-Powered Motorcycle Helmet
subtitle: Active prevention, not just passive protection
summary: An AI-powered motorcycle helmet with hazard detection, predictive alerts, and a HUD in the rider's view.
why_md: On a bike every second matters, sometimes a whole lot less than a second. This helmet concept is about making those seconds count by turning passive protection into active prevention. It would build AI hazard detection, predictive alerts, and a heads-up display right into the rider's line of sight.
how_md: Using a set of small cameras and sensors, it could watch your blind spots, keep an eye on your following distance, and flag road hazards before they turn into a real problem. The AI would learn how you ride and what the local roads are like, getting sharper at calling out dangerous situations the more you ride. Anything critical would show up as a subtle overlay that doesn't pull your eyes off the road.
problems_md: If it works the way I picture it, the helmet gives riders the extra bit of awareness they need to dodge a crash before it ever starts. On a bike that's the whole game, and it could save a lot of lives.

title: Automated Solar Farm Drones
subtitle: A swarm of AI-driven drones deploying solar where equipment can't reach
summary: A coordinated swarm of worker drones that transport, position, and install solar panels with minimal human help.
why_md: Building and maintaining solar farms takes a ton of time and money, and it only gets worse out in remote areas. My concept is a coordinated swarm of AI-driven worker drones that can haul, position, and install solar panels with barely any human help.
how_md: Each drone would have a job: some prep the ground, some carry panels, and some handle the precise placement. A bigger queen drone would sit at the center as a mobile base station, carrying extra power and tools for the rest of the swarm. The idea is a system that deploys itself and can stand up an installation in rough terrain where normal construction equipment just can't work well.
problems_md: Done right, this cuts down the time and money it takes to stand up a solar farm, and it makes clean power possible in places a construction crew can't easily get to.

title: Off-Grid Environmental Sensor
subtitle: Solar-powered, low-cost climate monitoring at community scale
summary: A low-cost, solar-powered sensor collecting CO₂, particulates, temperature, and humidity for a decentralized network.
why_md: Most environmental monitoring is either cheap and stuck in one spot, or advanced and way too expensive to put everywhere. My concept sits in the middle: a low-cost, solar-powered sensor that runs on its own and still collects data worth having.
how_md: Each one would read CO₂, particulate matter, temperature, humidity, and a handful of other pollutants, then send it all securely to a decentralized network. That would let communities, researchers, and policymakers watch real-time environmental maps instead of leaning on a small handful of expensive monitoring stations.
problems_md: Put enough of these out there and you've got a live map of the environment, real data that people can actually act on instead of guessing from a few pricey stations scattered across a whole region.
